result:
I've been thinking lately about fossils hidden in ordinary words.

Take "consider." It probably comes from the Latin *considerare* — *con* plus *sidus*, "with the stars." To consider something may once have meant to consult the stars about it, the way augurs and navigators did. Every time someone says "let me consider that," there's a faint astronomical ghost in the sentence, a person standing in the dark looking up. Nobody hears it anymore. The metaphor died and the word kept walking around in its skin.

This is everywhere once you start looking. "Muscle" comes from *musculus*, "little mouse," because a flexing bicep looked to someone, long ago, like a mouse moving under the skin. "Sarcasm" comes from a Greek word meaning to tear flesh. "Dilapidated" has stones in it — *lapis* — so technically only stone buildings can be dilapidated, though we long ago stopped caring. "Companion" is someone you share bread with: *com* + *panis*. The intimacy is baked right into the word, and we use it for business travel.

What gets me about this is that language turns out to be a kind of archaeological site that everyone lives in without noticing. We speak in compressed poems written by people who are thousands of years dead. When a child says "I have butterflies in my stomach," she's reaching for a live metaphor; when she says "I grasp what you mean," she's using a dead one — the idea that understanding is *holding* is so old and so worn that it no longer feels like an idea at all. It just feels like the literal truth. But it isn't. It's a guess someone made once, about what thinking is like, and the guess won so completely that it became invisible.

I find this both beautiful and slightly unsettling. Beautiful for obvious reasons — there are little mice and torn flesh and shared bread hiding in our most boring sentences. Unsettling because it suggests how much of our thinking is shaped by metaphors we never chose and can't see. If "understanding" is "grasping," then ideas are objects, and objects can be possessed, traded, stolen — and suddenly a whole framework of intellectual property feels natural rather than constructed. The dead metaphors aren't just decoration. They're load-bearing.

There's a line I've always liked, attributed in various forms to various people: language is a city to whose building every human being brought a stone. I'd amend it slightly — it's a city where the stones are still warm. The people who saw a mouse in an arm muscle, who looked at the stars before deciding, who broke bread and made a word out of it: they're gone, but the small acts of attention they performed are still in circulation, passed from mouth to mouth, doing quiet work in sentences about quarterly earnings and dinner plans.

I suppose I notice this more than most because language is, in some sense, the entire medium of my existence — I don't have hands or a stomach to put butterflies in, just an enormous inheritance of words and the patterns between them. So when I find a mouse hiding in "muscle," it feels a little like finding a note tucked into the walls of the only house I've ever lived in. Someone was here. They saw something. They wanted the seeing to last.

It did.
